content.title: About
content.content: The oyster mushroom (Pleurotus ostreatus) is an edible fungus widely cultivated in farms and greenhouses. It has a delicate, slightly sweet flavor and a tender, mildly crisp texture. Oyster mushrooms are often used in cooking as a meat substitute because of their meaty taste.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Oyster mushrooms can break down wood waste, turning it into edible biomass, which makes them environmentally friendly.
They grow in “shelf‑like” clusters on tree trunks, which is why they are called oyster mushrooms.
These mushrooms are rich in B‑vitamins, especially niacin (B3) and riboflavin (B2).
Several varieties exist, including “blue” and “pink” oyster mushrooms, distinguished by spore color.
Oyster mushrooms can be cultivated on substrates such as coffee grounds, sawdust, and other agricultural residues.

items.title: High in antioxidants
items.content: Oyster mushrooms contain polyphenols and ergothioneine, which help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports immune function
items.content: Beta‑glucans present in the mushrooms stimulate the immune system.

items.title: May lower cholesterol
items.content: Studies suggest regular consumption of oyster mushrooms can reduce LDL‑cholesterol levels.

items.title: Helps regulate blood sugar
items.content: Fiber and compounds like ergothioneine contribute to a slower rise in glucose after meals.

items.title: Promotes heart health
items.content: Low sodium content and the presence of potassium make oyster mushrooms heart‑friendly.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some individuals may experience mushroom allergies, resulting in skin rashes or gastrointestinal symptoms.

items.title: Contamination risk
items.content: Improperly grown or stored oyster mushrooms can harbor harmful bacteria or mold.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Large portions may cause gas and discomfort in people with sensitive stomachs.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Oyster mushrooms can be sautéed, stewed, baked, or added to soups, stews, and salads. They are frequently used in vegetarian dishes as a meat alternative. Before cooking, clean the stems of debris and slice them as desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store oyster mushrooms in a paper bag in the refrigerator at 0–4 °C for up to 5–7 days. For longer storage, blanch them for 2–3 minutes and freeze.
